newsitem.title: UK: Britain's Major struggles to improve party image.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Major struggles to improve party image.

text.p: British Prime Minister John Major embarks on the last month of campaigning on Tuesday facing the daunting task of cleansing his party's tainted image before polling day on May 1.

Major is struggling to shift the focus of the campaign away from a series of scandals in his Conservative Party. But he is being hindered by the refusal of two Conservatives to resign over sleaze allegations.
The prime minister appears to have the backing of opposition leader Tony Blair who said on Monday he wanted to get away from the sleaze allegations and onto policy.
"I do not want this election fought on negative issues. I want it fought on the policies that we offer to the people of our country," Blair told supporters from his Labour Party.
But behind the scenes, Labour officials made clear they won't easily drop the sleaze issue which has given them an unexpected boost in the two weeks since Major announced the election date.
Ten Conservative MPs are under investigation by a parliamentary committee into allegations that they accepted hefty cash sums in exchange for asking questions in the House of Commons (lower house).
The committee's report will not be published until after the election and Labour has accused Major of dismissing parliament early so that its findings will not be made public before polling day.
One of the MPs under investigation, Neil Hamilton, has defied senior party figures' calls for him to resign over claims he accepted money from Harrods owner Mohammed Al-Fayed.
Another Conservative resigned last week over the "cash for questions" allegations while two stood down over claims of scandal in their private lives.
Yet another MP, Piers Merchant, accused of having an extra-marital affair with a 17-year-old nightclub hostess, is also resisting pressure to resign.
Merchant and Hamilton both have the support of their local parties and Major on Monday appeared to have shifted away from his earlier appeals to the two to stand down.
Major told local party officials in a letter that they had the right to choose their own candidates but made clear the day of reckoning would come after the "cash for questions" report is published.
"The House of Commons has draconian powers. The Conservative Party will support their use if criticism is severe enough to merit it," Major wrote.
Blair's deputy, John Prescott, was scathing of Major's attempt to defuse the sleaze row.

"If Mr Major thinks that this letter draws a line under the issue he is wrong. While he fails to give leadership, sleaze will continue to dominate this election because the state of the Tory (Conservative) party and the weakness of John Major are of vital importance to everyone casting a vote on May 1," Prescott said.

Despite an opinion poll lead of over 20 points, Labour has resisted complacency about its chances and Blair resumes the campaign trail on Tuesday hoping to challenge the Conservatives' greatest asset -- Major himself, whom polls show is much more popular than his party.
Major is credited with having turned around Conservative fortunes in the 1992 national election when he began giving impromptu speeches in the streets from a battered soapbox.
Labour officials said Blair will bring out his answer to Major's soapbox on Tuesday when he makes speeches from a "people's platform" attached to his campaign tour bus.
Blair will be working to dispel fears that Labour still harbours left-wing tax-and-spend instincts, they said.
"The big question of the campaign is about the state of the Labour Party," an aide said. "That is the question Tony intends to answer between now and May 1."
